items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the breakdown or decay of rock in situ, at or near the Earth’s surface”.
items.answer: Weathering
items.markingKey: Weathering: the breakdown or decay of rock in situ, at or near the Earth’s surface. [1]

items.stem: Explain how freeze-thaw weathering breaks down rock.
items.answer: Water enters joints and pores; on freezing it expands by about 9%, exerting pressure; on thawing water penetrates further; repeated cycles widen cracks until fragments break off, forming scree.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Explain how pressure release can cause rocks to break up.
items.answer: When overlying rock is removed by erosion, the confining pressure falls; the rock expands and cracks develop parallel to the surface (sheet joints), allowing other weathering to act.

Suggest why air temperature data may not represent conditions inside rock cracks.
items.answer: Rock surfaces heat and cool differently from air (sun, shade, aspect); snow insulates; temperatures within cracks lag behind air temperature.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that physical weathering is more important than chemical weathering in shaping landscapes in cold environments.
items.answer: For: Freeze-thaw produces scree, blockfields and tors in periglacial areas; ice wedges and frost heave disturb soils. Against: Chemical weathering continues at low rates (carbonation is enhanced because cold water holds more CO₂); biological weathering by lichens; limestone pavements show solution. Conclusion: Physical weathering dominates in cold, dry environments, but chemical weathering is significant where water is abundant.

items.answer: Freeze-thaw (frost shattering)

items.stem: A student writes: “Freeze-thaw is most effective in places with permanently frozen ground.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It needs repeated cycles of freezing and thawing; permanently frozen ground has few cycles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why salt weathering is important in hot deserts.
items.answer: Saline groundwater is drawn to the surface by capillary action; evaporation causes salt crystals to grow in pores, exerting pressure; heating also expands salts.

items.answer: (a) Repeated freezing of water in joints prises off angular fragments, which fall and accumulate at the base of cliffs at about 35°. (b) Rock surfaces heat and cool differently from air (sun, shade, aspect); snow insulates; temperatures within cracks lag behind air temperature.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the reaction of rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide (carbonic acid) with calcium carbonate in limestone to form soluble calcium bicarbonate”.
items.answer: Carbonation
items.markingKey: Carbonation: the reaction of rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide (carbonic acid) with calcium carbonate in limestone to form soluble calcium bicarbonate. [1]

items.stem: Explain why carbonation can be more rapid in cold climates than might be expected.
items.answer: Cold water can hold more dissolved carbon dioxide, so rainwater and meltwater are more acidic; soils with decaying vegetation add CO₂.

items.stem: Explain how hydrolysis breaks down granite.
items.answer: Hydrogen ions in water react with feldspar crystals, converting them into soft clay minerals (kaolinite); quartz grains are released, so the rock crumbles (grus).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reaction; 1 mark clay; 1 mark disintegration [3]

items.stem: Assume that rates of chemical weathering double for every 10 °C rise in temperature. The mean annual temperature at a station in Canada is 0 °C and at a station in Brazil is 20 °C, and both have abundant moisture. Suggest why the predicted difference may not be found in reality.
items.answer: Rock type, vegetation, water supply, time and removal of weathered material also affect rates; some reactions (carbonation) are faster in cold water.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that chemical weathering is the most important type of weathering in all environments?
items.answer: For: Chemical weathering dominates in the humid tropics (weathering profiles over 60 m deep); carbonation shapes limestone landscapes worldwide; hydrolysis produces clays. Against: In cold and arid environments physical weathering (freeze-thaw, salt crystal growth) dominates because water or warmth is limited; biological weathering matters in vegetated areas. Conclusion: Chemical weathering is the most widespread and effective globally, but not in all environments.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “carbonation”?
options: The reaction of rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide (carbonic acid) with calcium carbonate in limestone to form soluble calcium bicarbonate.
The reaction of minerals, especially iron, with oxygen, producing red-brown iron oxides that weaken rock.
The reaction between rock minerals and water, especially the breakdown of feldspar in granite to form clay (kaolinite).
The absorption of water into the structure of minerals, causing them to swell.
items.answer: The reaction of rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide (carbonic acid) with calcium carbonate in limestone to form soluble calcium bicarbonate.
items.markingKey: Carbonation: the reaction of rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide (carbonic acid) with calcium carbonate in limestone to form soluble calcium bicarbonate. [1]

items.stem: Explain the ways in which plants and animals contribute to weathering.
items.answer: Roots grow into cracks and exert pressure; lichens and mosses secrete organic acids (chelation); decaying vegetation adds CO₂ and humic acids; burrowing animals expose fresh rock.

items.stem: Explain how rock structure influences the rate of weathering.
items.answer: Joints, bedding planes and faults allow water to enter, increasing the surface area for weathering; closely jointed rock weathers faster; permeable rock allows water to penetrate deeply.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain how vegetation affects weathering.
items.answer: Roots wedge open cracks; decaying vegetation releases humic acids and CO₂, increasing chemical weathering; vegetation keeps the ground moist; but it can also protect rock from extremes of temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Assess the view that climate is the most important factor affecting the type and rate of weathering. In your answer you may refer to jointing, vegetation and rock type.
items.answer: For: The Peltier diagram shows how temperature and rainfall determine whether chemical weathering, frost action or slight weathering dominates. Against: Rock type (mineral composition, jointing, permeability), vegetation, relief and time strongly influence rates; limestone and granite weather very differently in the same climate. Conclusion: Climate largely determines the type of weathering, but rock characteristics often control the rate locally.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how rock structure influences the rate of weathering. (b) A revision website states: “Mean annual figures can hide important seasonal variations in weathering conditions.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Joints, bedding planes and faults allow water to enter, increasing the surface area for weathering; closely jointed rock weathers faster; permeable rock allows water to penetrate deeply. items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the breaking of rock by the pressure of salt crystals growing in pores and cracks as saline water evaporates”.
items.answer: Salt crystal growth

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how pressure release can cause rocks to break up. (b) A revision website states: “Laboratory experiments suggest heating and cooling alone may not break dry rock.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) When overlying rock is removed by erosion, the confining pressure falls; the rock expands and cracks develop parallel to the surface (sheet joints), allowing other weathering to act. (b) Correct. Griggs’s experiments showed little effect without water, so moisture and salts are thought to be important in exfoliation.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why salt weathering is important in hot deserts. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Physical weathering increases the surface area exposed to chemical weathering.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Saline groundwater is drawn to the surface by capillary action; evaporation causes salt crystals to grow in pores, exerting pressure; heating also expands salts. (b) Correct. Breaking rock into smaller pieces exposes more surface to water and acids.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

(a) Explain how freeze-thaw weathering produces scree slopes. (b) Suggest why air temperature data may not represent conditions inside rock cracks.
items.answer: (a) Repeated freezing of water in joints prises off angular fragments, which fall and accumulate at the base of cliffs at about 35°. (b) Rock surfaces heat and cool differently from air (sun, shade, aspect); snow insulates; temperatures within cracks lag behind air temperature.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that physical weathering is more important than chemical weathering in shaping landscapes in cold environments?
items.answer: For: Freeze-thaw produces scree, blockfields and tors in periglacial areas; ice wedges and frost heave disturb soils. Against: Chemical weathering continues at low rates (carbonation is enhanced because cold water holds more CO₂); biological weathering by lichens; limestone pavements show solution. Conclusion: Physical weathering dominates in cold, dry environments, but chemical weathering is significant where water is abundant.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the ways in which plants and animals contribute to weathering. (b) A revision website states: “Biological weathering can be both physical and chemical.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Assume that rates of chemical weathering double for every 10 °C rise in temperature. The mean annual temperature at a station in the Alps is 0 °C and at a station in Ghana is 20 °C, and both have abundant moisture. Name and describe one chemical weathering process that affects granite.
items.answer: Hydrolysis: feldspars react with water to form kaolinite clay, releasing quartz grains.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that chemical weathering is the most important type of weathering in all environments. In your answer you may refer to rock type, deserts and periglacial areas.
items.answer: For: Chemical weathering dominates in the humid tropics (weathering profiles over 60 m deep); carbonation shapes limestone landscapes worldwide; hydrolysis produces clays. Against: In cold and arid environments physical weathering (freeze-thaw, salt crystal growth) dominates because water or warmth is limited; biological weathering matters in vegetated areas. Conclusion: Chemical weathering is the most widespread and effective globally, but not in all environments.
